issues.legal_issue: A public university’s delay in filing an intra-court appeal is not condonable when the extensive delay is supported only by inadequate administrative explanations and the surrounding circumstances show that the delay was not reasonably accounted for.
material_facts: The university filed its intra-court appeal 916 days after dismissal of its writ petition.
The university attributed the delay to deliberations by its authorities, the vacancy in the Vice-Chancellor’s office, committee reports, and the need for Executive Council approval.

The Vice-Chancellor who had overseen the writ proceedings remained in office for about six months after the judgment, and the Executive Council approved filing the appeal more than a year before it was filed.
The record did not adequately explain the delay at each stage, including the substantial period after the Executive Council’s approval.
The public transport body had received substantial funds for the project, which were being used for metro services to the public.
issues.conclusion: The university failed to establish sufficient cause for the 916-day delay, and the High Court was justified in refusing to condone it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits condonation where sufficient cause is shown. Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Katiji supports a liberal, justice-oriented approach, but does not make condonation automatic; Postmaster General v. Living Media India Ltd. establishes that routine administrative delay is insufficient without a reasonable explanation and bona fide effort. The Court also relied on the principle that accrued consequences and the facts of each case must be weighed carefully.

rule.if: delayed_appeal and extensive_appeal_delay and institutional_process_cited and (official_available_during_appeal_window or approval_preceded_filing_substantially) and later_filing_gap_unaccounted and public_project_funds_already_received

predicates.delayed_appeal: A litigant filed an appeal after the prescribed time had passed.
predicates.extensive_appeal_delay: The appeal was filed after a substantial period of delay.
predicates.institutional_process_cited: The public institution attributed the delay to internal deliberations, staffing circumstances, or approval procedures.
predicates.official_available_during_appeal_window: The official responsible for the institution’s affairs remained in office for a substantial part of the period available to file the appeal.
predicates.approval_preceded_filing_substantially: The institution’s competent body approved filing the appeal well before the appeal was actually filed.
predicates.later_filing_gap_unaccounted: The institution did not give a reasonable account of the substantial period between approval and filing.
predicates.public_project_funds_already_received: A public body had already received funds connected with the project and was using them for a public service.

issues.definition: When a delayed appeal follows an extensive and inadequately explained delay, including an unexplained gap after internal approval, and the project has public consequences, condonation is denied.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to public action is barred by laches when the action was publicly knowable well before the petition and the petitioner did not act despite events that should have prompted a challenge.
material_facts: The land was converted to residential use years before the university filed its writ petition.
The public transport body invited bids and conducted a public auction for the land before the petition was filed.
Related litigation concerning the residential development had already occurred, and the development was in the public domain.
The university filed its writ petition years after the conversion and auction, and the writ court found that it suffered from delay and laches.
issues.conclusion: The writ court was justified in finding that the university’s writ petition was hit by delay and laches.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the equitable principles governing delay and laches and cited M/s Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Company Ltd. v. District Board, Bhojpur for the test that a petitioner should approach the court before a parallel right is created and that the lapse of time should not be attributable to laches or negligence. The Court considered the public availability of the development and the petitioner’s failure to act when events should have prompted it to do so.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_public_action and public_action_preceded_petition_substantially and public_events_signalled_the_challenge and petitioner_failed_to_act_promptly

predicates.writ_challenge_to_public_action: A petitioner brought a writ proceeding challenging action taken by a public authority.
predicates.public_action_preceded_petition_substant: The challenged action occurred a substantial time before the petitioner filed the writ proceeding.
predicates.public_events_signalled_the_challenge: Publicly visible steps or related proceedings indicated the development or action that the petitioner later challenged.
predicates.petitioner_failed_to_act_promptly: The petitioner did not bring the challenge promptly after those events occurred.

issues.definition: When a petitioner challenges public action only after substantial delay despite public events signalling the action, the writ petition is barred by laches.

issues.legal_issue: A public body seeking condonation of delay is subject to the same standard as any other litigant and receives no special limitation treatment because of its status.
material_facts: The applicant seeking condonation was a public university.
The university relied in part on its institutional decision-making procedures and administrative circumstances to explain the delay.
The Court assessed the explanation and consequences of delay by reference to the circumstances of the case rather than the applicant’s public status.
issues.conclusion: The university was not entitled to a different or more favourable standard for condonation merely because it was a public body.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies the sufficient-cause standard without distinguishing between public and private litigants. Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Katiji states that litigants are to be treated even-handedly, while Postmaster General v. Living Media India Ltd. confirms that government bodies are bound by limitation and cannot rely on routine bureaucratic explanations alone.

predicates.delay_condonation_application: A litigant asked a court to excuse delay in filing a proceeding.
predicates.public_body_applicant: The litigant seeking to excuse the delay was a public institution or government body.

issues.definition: When a public body asks a court to excuse filing delay, the same condonation standard applies to it as to other litigants.
